Deductions generally allowed in the Swiss cantons include: - Professional expenses and labour costs (professional clothing, tools, travel for employees) - Interest on mortgage loans (for own homes) - Health insurance premiums (LAMal/KVG, the mandatory coverage for Swiss residents) - Contributions to [previdenza professionale](nav:pension) (LPP/BVG, the mandatory second pillar) - Payments to the third pillar (social security savings accounts 3a), within annual indexed ceilings every year - Previous cantonal taxes (in some cantons), union and associative contributions

## In a nutshell - Family allowances: monthly allowance for each dependent child in Switzerland - Appenzello Esterno applies the federal regime through a cantonal compensation fund - Application at the cashier affiliated to the employer or at the cantonal office
## Key facts - **What**: Family allowances (Familienzulagen) + training allowances for children in education - When: From the first day of the month of birth until the age of 25 (or end of training) - Where: Canton Appenzello Outer, north-eastern Switzerland - Who: Parents employed, self-employed, farmers with Swiss residence - Amount: Determined by federal law and cantonal decisions (variable by canton)
The Swiss system of family allowances is one of the pillars of national social security. These are monthly subsidies paid to parents who have dependent children, designed to cover part of the costs related to education, nutrition and development.
In the Canton of Appenzell Outermost, as in all Swiss cantons, family allowances are based on a federal regulatory framework, but find practical operation through cantonal compensation funds. This model makes it possible to maintain national cohesion while adapting the amounts and procedures to local realities.
### The federal-cantonal system of family allowances
Family allowances in Switzerland are not a discretionary benefit: they constitute a social right guaranteed by federal law to anyone who works ### Monthly amounts and cantonal variability
The amounts of family allowances are fixed by cantonal legislation and vary significantly from one canton to another. Outer Appenzel, like all Swiss cantons, autonomously determines the amounts applicable for: - **Child allowances **: paid monthly for each child up to a predetermined age (generally 16 years for children in general education) - Training allowances: amounts increased during periods of apprenticeship, vocational school or recognised universities, up to the age of 25
The exact amounts in force in the External Appenzell must be consulted directly at the competent compensation fund or on the canton portal, as these are adapted annually to correspond to the evolution of the cost of living and local political decisions.
### Duration and termination of the right
The right to family allowances starts from the first day of the month in which the child is born (or from the month in which the parent acquires residence in Switzerland, whichever is the later). The ordinary term corresponds to the child's 25th birthday.
However, if the child continues in a recognized training (apprenticeship, cantonal vocational school or university) beyond the age of 25, the training allowances continue until the end of the training itself. In the case of children with a disability recognised by the AI, the payment may be extended according to specific conditions.

The presentation of the family allowance application in Appenzello Esterno follows a standardized procedure, divided into four main phases.
Step 1: Identify the competent compensation fund
Most Swiss employers are affiliated with a compensation fund for a specific sector (industry, commerce and services, agriculture, domestic enterprises). If the employer is affiliated with one of these funds, the application must be submitted to that fund.
If the employer is not affiliated with any private compensation fund, the application must be submitted directly to the Appenzello Esterno cantonal compensation fund (Ausgleichskasse Appenzell Ausserrhoden). Contacts are available on the website www.ar.ch.
Step 2: Prepare the required documentation
To advance the application, the following documents must be gathered: - Birth certificate of the children (authentic copy) - Residence certificate in the Appenzello Esterno canton - Valid identification document of the applicant - Proof of occupational situation (employment contract for employees; AVS income statement for self-employed; extract from the commercial register for individual companies) - In the case of separated or divorced parents: court ruling attesting to the child's custody - In the case of unmarried paternity: registered declaration of paternity in the civil register
**Step 3: Submit the application
The application can be submitted through two channels: - Physical counter: at the competent compensation fund, during official opening hours - Online: many Swiss funds, including that of Appenzello Esterno, offer downloadable digital forms from the official website, with the possibility of telematic transmission
It is recommended to submit the application simultaneously with the child's birth or the start of the employment relationship, to avoid losing retroactive rights.
Step 4: Elaboration and first payment
Once the complete application with all documents has been received, the fund will process it within the prescribed terms (usually 30-60 days). The first allowance is paid in the month following the approval of the application, by bank transfer to the account indicated by the applicant.
### Continuity and variations over time
Once approved, the application remains active, and allowances are paid automatically every month until the right expires (25th birthday or end of training). It is not necessary to renew the application annually.
However, it is essential to notify the compensation fund promptly of any change in situation that may affect the right: - Birth of additional children - Change of employer or affiliated fund - Transfer of residence to another Swiss canton - End of training or change of school cycle - Separation, divorce, or modification of custody
Omitting these notifications may result in unjustified interruptions or errors in payments.

## In a nutshell - Permit L allows work for up to 12 months, renewable if contract continues - Bound to specific employer, not transferable to other employers - Extension requests a new application from the cantonal office before the deadline - Switching to permit B depends on occupational continuity and employer willingness
## Key facts - **What**: L permit (short duration for foreign workers) - When: Valid 12 months from release, renewable - Where: Canton Appenzello Outer (eastern Switzerland) - Who: Cantonal Office for Migration + Federal SEM (State Secretariat for Migration) - Requirement: Employment contract with employer resident in Switzerland
The short-term L permit is the central regulatory instrument for the recruitment of foreign workers in the Swiss cantons. In the canton of Appenzello Esterno, economically oriented to the manufacturing and service sectors, the L permit allows employers to take on skills from abroad with defined administrative procedures and predetermined times.
The maximum duration of the L permit is 12 calendar months, according to the federal regulations of the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM). This means that the foreign worker obtains a residence title limited in time, strictly bound to the employment contract and the specific employer who sponsored the application.
### Federal and cantonal jurisdiction
In Outer Appenzell, as in all Swiss cantons, the management of permits follows a double ### Validity, renewal and extension
The L permit is valid for 12 months from the date of issue. This period ** is not automatically renewable**: the extension depends on the continuity of the employment relationship and the employer's willingness to maintain the hiring.
In Appenzello Esterno, renewal does not constitute a right acquired by the worker. Approximately 2-3 months before the expiry of the L permit, the employer must assess whether it intends to continue hiring. If yes, you must submit a new renewal application to the cantonal migration office, again providing the necessary documentation (updated contract, certificates of good life, attestations of qualifications).
The cantonal office re-examines the application according to the current federal and cantonal criteria: priority for the local labour market, absence of Swiss unemployed or citizens with a B permit for the same type of job, compliance with the sector's market wages. If the economic situation has changed (e.g. sector crisis, rising unemployment), renewal may be refused even if the employer intends to continue hiring.
### Transition to permit B (residence)
Once the L permit has expired, the foreign worker is not automatically entitled to a B (residence) permit. However, if the employment relationship continues and the employer wishes to maintain the hiring, it is possible to apply for a conversion from L permit to B permit.

Step 1: Preliminary check at the canton
The employer contacts the Appenzello Esterno canton migration office to clarify the current requirements. Each canton has slightly different acceptance criteria based on the local labor market and occupational priorities. It is useful to check directly which sectors are currently open to the L permit and which documentation is required.
**Step 2: Collection of documentation**
The following documents are required (with variations by canton):
- Signed employment contract between the employer and foreign worker (must specify position, hours, salary, duration) - Certificate of good conduct/morality of the candidate foreigner (required by the country of origin or SEM) - Documentation attesting professional qualifications (diplomas, certificates, experience certificates) - Identification documents and valid passport - Proof of the employer's contribution capacity (if required by the canton)
The employer is responsible for collecting the documentation before submission.
Step 3: Submission of the application
The formal request is submitted to the Appenzello Esterno canton migration office. The office then transmits it to the federal SEM for final approval. It is recommended to keep a copy of the application and the receipt of submission.
Step 4: Instruction and approval
The instruction times are approximately 2-4 weeks for simple cases (e.g. seasonal employment clearly motivated, candidate from a country with facilitated agreements). More complex cases may require 6-8 weeks or more.
Step 5: Issuance of the L permit
Once approved, the application generates the formal L permit. The document is notified to the employer. The foreign worker can then enter or remain in Switzerland for the period of validity (12 months).
### Management of expiration and renewal
About 2-3 months before the L permit expiration, the employer should assess whether to renew. If they intend to maintain the employment:
- Contact the cantonal office again - Submit a new renewal application (with updated documentation) - Follow the same instruction procedure
If the employer does not renew, the worker has two options:
1. Leave the Swiss territory by the date of expiration of the permit 2. Find a new employer willing to sponsor a new L permit
The L permit does not allow the worker to remain in Switzerland without work after the expiration date.
### Where to contact in Appenzello Esterno
- Appenzello Esterno canton migration office: manages L permits at the cantonal level, evaluates conformity with local requirements, instructs first-level applications - Federal Migration Office (SEM): supervises general criteria, definitively approves permits on cantonal referral, manages federal matters of principle
For specific questions about the L permit and deadlines in Appenzello Esterno, the employer or their HR consultant should directly contact the cantonal office, which provides updated information on forms, administrative deadlines, and current seasonal criteria.
### Fiscal and social security implications
A frequently overlooked aspect is that a worker with an L permit, once employed in Switzerland, is subject to the same fiscal and social security obligations as any resident employee:
- AVS/AI/IPG: 5.3% at the expense of the employee, 10.6% total with employer contribution - Unemployment insurance (AD/AC): 1.1% up to annual maximum - LAMal/KVG (health insurance): mandatory within 3 months of arrival, premium per capita based on age and chosen franchise (300–2,500 CHF for adults) - Federal, cantonal, and communal taxes: according to income bracket and cantonal domicile
The employer is responsible for regular contributions and withholding taxes. ### The Swiss Academies Report
The Swiss Academies of Sciences have published a report estimating the costs of building a new nuclear power plant in Switzerland. The figure is surprisingly large: between 14 and 43 billion francs. How was it possible to reach such a wide range? The researchers examined two models of reactors of different sizes, calculating how costs could evolve under different conditions.
The starting costs used by the researchers are based on the current offers for large reactors, which are around 11,500 and 12,000 francs per kilowatt of power. From this basis, the scientists worked out two distinct scenarios.

A crucial question naturally arises: could the Swiss private sector, represented by companies such as Axpo and BKW, directly finance such a venture? According to the report, the answer is very unlikely. The researchers believe that the construction of a new nuclear power plant in Switzerland will require considerable state support.
Specific financial risks are hardly sustainable by private actors alone. These include: extremely high initial investments (tens of billions), multi-year construction times without revenue, and uncertain electricity prices in the long amortization phase (which can last decades). In fact, international experiences show that in recent years it has only been possible to find private investors if the State has strongly mitigated the risks.
An additional element further complicates the Swiss framework: since potential managers such as Axpo and BKW are wholly or partially owned by the Cantons, in an investment of this caliber the public sector would still be indirectly involved and would help to bear the financial risks. In other words, even a 'private' solution would not really be: the cantonal public sector would remain a de facto co-investor.

According to the report, the tender should be issued as early as the early 1930s if the goal is to provide electricity by the early 1950s. This means that the time window for a political decision is very narrow. A large nuclear power plant construction cycle typically takes 10-15 years, sometimes more with the delays seen in international projects. There are no wide margins for improvisation.
The fundamental assumption is a political decision of principle. Today this is still pending: the February 2026 referendum represents the first step of a democratic consultation on a strategic issue for Switzerland.
### Potential Contractors
In the event of an investment decision by the mid-2030s, the choice will presumably fall mainly on large third-generation water-cooled reactors (III/III+). Currently, only EDF/Framatome (France) and Westinghouse (United States) are in the running as contractors for Switzerland. Although they are currently building the most reactors worldwide, Chinese state groups (CNG, CNNC) and Russian (Rosatom) are excluded from Europe and Switzerland for geopolitical reasons. The South Korean KEPCO/KHNP, which certainly has experience, cannot currently offer its reactors in Europe independently due to a legal dispute with Westinghouse.
### And the Small Modular Reactors?
An alternative solution could come from the so-called 'mini-reactors' (Small Modular Reactors, SMR). However, the current answer is negative: there are no concrete empirical data on construction times and actual costs for SMR. Outside of China and Russia, this technology is mostly still in development or in the early stages of prototyping. A large project planned by the US producer NuScale was even abandoned before construction began due to a significant increase in cost predictions. For a political decision by Switzerland in the short term, SMR therefore do not offer a sufficiently solid economic data base.
### What to do now
Swiss citizens will have to express themselves in February 2026 on the referendum against the abolition of the ban on building new power plants. Those who want to delve deeper into the economic implications of such a decision can consult the analyses published by the Swiss Academies of Sciences and the Federal Council. The law of rental property in Switzerland, including the Canton of Schaffhausen, is governed by the Code of Obligations (CO) articles 253 and following. These federal laws define uniform rights and obligations for tenants and landlords across all Swiss cantons, ensuring stable legal protection regardless of region.
One of the key provisions concerns the deposit, also known as the guarantee deposit: the landlord can retain a maximum amount equal to three months' rent as a guarantee. This deposit must be made in a blocked account held in the tenant's name, ensuring that the amount remains available to the tenant and cannot be confused with the landlord's accounts or used for other purposes.
The termination of the rental contract by the landlord is only valid if communicated through the official cantonal form. Different forms, verbal communications, informal emails, or unofficial letters have no legal value, even if the landlord believes they have correctly notified the contract. This formal requirement protects the tenant from ambiguous interpretations.
To contest the initial rent proposed by the landlord, the tenant has a 30-day deadline to turn to the conciliation authority for rental disputes in the canton. This procedure is mandatory before resorting to court and is completely free of charge.

### The deposit and the blocked account
The regulation of the deposit is designed to protect the tenant: the money does not remain in the landlord's coffers, but in a separate account that the tenant can control at any time. At the end of the contract, the landlord is obliged to return the deposit within 30 days, deducting only the amounts justified by proven damages or documented arrears.
If the landlord believes that there are rights to compensation (costs for damages to the walls, extraordinary cleaning costs, unmade repairs by the tenant), they must communicate the details of the deductions before retaining part of the deposit. Any arbitrary or unmotivated retention is contestable at the conciliation authority within 30 days. ### How the termination of the contract works in Sciaffusa, Switzerland, and throughout the country, the landlord who intends to terminate the contract must use the official cantonal form. This document contains the mandatory fields (names of the parties, address of the property, precise date of the contract's end) and is available at the cantonal authority for conciliation in matters of rental or can be downloaded from the cantonal administration's website. The termination must be sent in writing, preferably by registered mail with return receipt, in order to have proof of delivery. A verbal communication during a conversation, an informal email, a message, or a letter on personal letterhead has no legal value and does not validly initiate the termination procedure. The legal terms for termination vary depending on the duration of the relationship: - **1 month** during the first year of the contract - 2 months from the second year to the ninth year - 3 months from the tenth year onwards These terms are peremptory: a termination that does not respect the times is null. The landlord cannot terminate the contract at will; they must follow the procedure and the terms prescribed by law. ### Procedure for contesting the initial rent If the tenant believes the initial rent is unjust, excessive compared to the prices in the area, or not in line with the quality and level of the property, they have exactly 30 days to submit an application to the conciliation authority. It is not necessary to resort to a lawyer for this phase: the form can be completed by the tenant themselves. The conciliation authority evaluates whether the proposed rent is congruent with local market prices, the condition of the property, the services provided, and the terms of the contract. If the authority finds grounds for contestation, it can mediate an agreement between the parties or issue a conciliation opinion that, if not appealed, becomes binding. Only after a failed attempt at conciliation can the tenant appeal to the cantonal court, with greater procedural burdens and legal costs. This two-tier system encourages a negotiated and rapid solution. ### The role of the conciliation authority in rental matters The conciliation authority is the neutral cantonal organ that mediates between tenant and landlord in all rental disputes. It receives applications on rent disputes, irregular terminations, unjustified security deposits, disputes over accessory expenses, and other conflicts related to rental. The response times vary by canton, but a complete conciliation procedure typically takes between two and three months. The authority has mediation powers: it can invite both parties to an informal meeting, listen to their reasons, and try to find a reciprocal agreement. If mediation fails, the authority issues a conciliation opinion (binding, subject to subsequent judicial appeal). Keep a copy: you will need it if you have to terminate the contract. 3. Document the condition of the property: at the time of entry, write a written inventory of the rooms (state of walls, floors, fixtures, installations), possibly accompanied by dated photos. This inventory becomes proof of the initial state and protects you from unjustified deductions at the end. 4. Check the rent within 30 days: if the rent seems high compared to other similar rentals in the area (same square footage, location, services), collect comparative data and contact the conciliation authority before the 30-day deadline expires. 5. Keep documentation of everything: keep the original signed contract, payment receipts, any written communications from the landlord. These documents are essential in case of disputes.

Some cantons make available informative brochures on rental law downloadable for free from the official website. Check the Sciaffusa portal to see if a local guide is available.

Do not accept verbal or informal cancellation forms: the landlord must use the official cantonal form. ### What is apprenticeship in Switzerland
Apprenticeship is the privileged vocational training path in the Swiss education system. It is based on the dual education model: the apprentice spends part of the week in the company (learning the practical trade) and part in the vocational school (acquiring theoretical and general skills). The apprentice's salary is set in the internship contract and increases progressively over the 3-4 years. There is no federal minimum wage in Switzerland, however many cantons, including Schaffhausen, have cantonal guidelines or collective bargaining agreements (CCLs) that define guiding minimum wages for traineeships. The Swiss Federal Office for Economic Supply (AEP) has announced that Switzerland will be able to draw on the transit gas pipeline from France to Italy if necessary, through the option called ITA.SWAPtion.26.
This measure represents a direct response to low reserve levels in EU Member States and uncertainties in international energy markets. Switzerland, we remember, has no seasonal gas storage of its own and is completely dependent on imports.

Switzerland has adopted a hierarchical protection mechanism in the event of a serious gas shortage. So-called 'unprotected' customers — mainly industries — would be subject to restrictions before vulnerable categories. "Protected" customers include hospitals, emergency services and families, ensuring continuity of essential service in a scenario of energy crisis.
This hierarchy is particularly relevant for Swiss industrial sectors, where even a temporary supply disruption could have significant economic impacts. Switzerland, Germany and Italy have signed a solidarity agreement that will enter into force if circumstances so require. In the event of a serious shortage and once all possible measures have been exhausted at national level, protected customers will be able to continue to receive gas supplies from these two European partners. The Ticino State Council launched a consultation on June 1, 2026 on the proposal for the attribution of hospital performance mandates in the acute care, rehabilitation, and psychiatry sectors. An inquiry by Matteo Quadranti, PLR group leader, questions the technical criteria used to determine the need underlying this planning.
At the center of the issue is the choice to rely on data from 2019 to estimate the need. When the consultative commission was established in 2022, these represented the most recent available: data from 2020 and 2021 had been compromised by the pandemic. Today, however, according to prio.swiss (one of the consulted organizations), this statistical base may not adequately reflect the current reality of the Ticino healthcare system.
Quadranti submits the State Council with a series of specific questions. Firstly, he asks to identify the criticisms emerged during the consultation procedure among the other actors of the healthcare system. Secondly, he raises the risk that a calculation of the need based on data now seven years old (at the time of the publication of the planning in 2026) may lead to an overestimation of the stationary offer necessary.
### The role of reforms in the healthcare sector
The PLR highlights a procedural aspect of relevance: the non-consideration of the normative and organizational evolutions of the last years, in particular the push towards the ambulatory and the implementation of the EFAS. If these changes are not incorporated into the calculation, the risk is of attributing a number of mandates higher than the effective need, with repercussions on healthcare costs.
The consultation remains open to the observations of the stakeholders. Quadranti finally poses a crucial procedural question: a planning built on potentially erroneous statistical bases may expose the Government to appeals, thus blocking its implementation for the next years and creating uncertainty for the Ticino healthcare sector. The response of the State Council to this inquiry will therefore be decisive in clarifying the trajectory of the cantonal hospital planning and its impact on the [LAMal](nav:health) for residents. ### Because outdated data weighs on planning

Between 2019 and 2026, the Ticino and national health system underwent significant transformations. In the period considered, EFAs was implemented and the push towards outpatient care accelerated, potentially reducing the demand for traditional beds. The availability of complete statistical data — clinical outcomes, number of hospitalizations, average length of stay, diagnoses — depends on the information systems of the cantons and the reporting obligations to the Confederation. Typically, these data have a 12-18 month lag compared to the reference period: 2024 data may be complete only in 2025-2026. It is therefore possible that, at the time of the summer consultation in 2026, the most recent available data would still be those of 2024 or 2023, and not yet those of 2025. ### What changes if the calculation is updated If the Government decides to update the hospital demand calculation based on post-pandemic data, the planning may be revised according to three scenarios: **Minimum scenario**: demand is lower than that calculated with 2019 data. Ambulatory care predominance reduces stationary demand. Reduced mandates, lower overall costs for LAMal. Medium scenario: demand remains similar to that calculated. Planning remains substantially unchanged compared to the initial proposal. Maximum scenario: demand is higher than estimated. Unforeseen clinical needs, increased population or clinical complexity. Increased mandates, potentially higher costs. Quadranti explicitly asks the Government where the most recent post-pandemic data sit in relation to these three scenarios, in order to evaluate whether the current planning reflects reality. ### Next steps and impact on the healthcare system The response of the State Council to this interrogation will be public and will contribute to defining the trajectory of Ticinese hospital planning. If the Government decides to update the calculation, this would involve a revision of the consultation and the implementation schedule. If, instead, it maintains the 2019 base, it will need to justify this choice and manage the risk of legal challenges. Swiss residents, particularly those in Ticino, have a direct interest in a solid and transparent hospital planning, as it affects the overall efficiency of LAMal and the premiums they pay to the sick funds. Greater clarity on the technical basis of the planning is therefore in the interest of all insured parties.

Zurich — The Swiss insurance sector closed 2025 in a state of robust financial soundness. This assessment was released today by the Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority (FINMA) through its annual report dedicated to the sector. Swiss insurance companies recorded an aggregate annual result of 24.4 billion francs in 2025, representing a dramatic 136% increase compared to the 14 billion francs registered in 2024.
Growth is not uniform across the various insurance branches. Non-life insurers achieved profits of 12.9 billion francs, while reinsurers reached 9.8 billion francs. On the gross premiums side, the picture is slightly different. Total volume decreased by 0.6%, stopping at 149 billion francs. However, trends vary considerably by branch: life insurers recorded a 3.7% increase in gross premiums, while property and casualty insurers posted a 2.8% increase. Reinsurers, conversely, suffered a 6.1% drop, mainly due to the appreciation of the Swiss franc against the US dollar, the euro, and the British pound. item.description: The price of unleaded petrol 95 exceeds 2 francs per litre for the first time since 2022. Diesel at CHF 2.27. The causes: conflicts in the Middle East and logistics crisis on the Rhine.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - 95 unleaded petrol: 2.02 CHF/litre, first pass since 2022 - Diesel at 2.27 CHF/litre; both +0.05 CHF in a week - Causes: Middle East conflicts, Rhine logistics, refining capacity
## Key facts - **What**: Historical gasoline price threshold exceeded - When: August 2026 (first time since 2022) - Where: Switzerland, national average - Who: TCS (Swiss Touring Club) - Petrol: 2.02 CHF/litre (+0.05 CHF weekly) - Diesel: CHF 2.27/litre (+0.05 CHF weekly) - Comparison 2022: CHF 2.31 (petrol) and CHF 2.40 (diesel)
The Swiss Touring Club (TCS) has announced an alarming new figure on the fuel front. The average price of unleaded petrol 95 has exceeded the critical threshold of 2 francs per litre for the first time since 2022. Specifically, the cost stands at 2.02 francs per litre on a national basis, with an increase of 5 cents recorded in just seven days.
Diesel advances at the same pace, reaching 2.27 francs per litre. Here too, the weekly increase is 5 cents. The announcement comes in a context of global energy price rises, with direct repercussions on the spending of Swiss households.
## # What drives prices up
The TCS has identified multiple causes behind the increase. Geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and reduced global refining capacities are the primary factors. To these are added the damage suffered by several ### The comparison with the 2022 peak
Although the increase is evident, it's useful to place the data in a historical context. In 2022, during the energy crisis following the war in Ukraine, unleaded gasoline 95 reached prices of up to 2.31 francs per liter, while diesel prices approached 2.40 francs. The current prices remain below the four-year highs, but the trend is clearly rising.
### The perfect logistical storm
What makes the situation particularly critical is the convergence of several unfavorable factors. It's not just a simple geopolitical tension — although that is serious — but a combination of phenomena that reinforce each other. The reduction in refining capacity has narrowed the global supply. Conflicts have added uncertainty to investments and directly hit some strategic facilities.
The Rhine drought, caused by adverse climate conditions, has crippled one of Europe's main logistical arteries for fuel transportation to Switzerland. Tanker ships cannot fully load due to insufficient depth. This means that less fuel passes from Rotterdam to Basel, creating a bottleneck that directly affects Swiss prices.
### Short-term prospects
The TCS does not offer reassuring prospects. The institute notes that in the short term, in light of the persistence of the geopolitical situation, the limited refining capacity, and the ongoing transportation problems, it is not reasonable to expect a significant drop in prices. Those who drive daily or rely on merchandise transportation will have to adapt to a structurally more expensive context in the medium term.
For those managing corporate fleets or operating in merchandise transportation, this represents an additional pressure on margins. [Logistics costs directly affect the final cost of consumer goods](nav:cost-of-living), with potential diffused inflationary reflections in the national economy.

Logistical costs for companies will inevitably increase. Prices for goods transported by road will face upward pressure. The public transportation and services sector will need to assess whether to pass on some of the costs to ticket and tariff prices.

item.title: Demographic slowdown in 2025: +0.8%
item.description: As of December 31, 2025, Switzerland has 9.127 million inhabitants. Growth slows to 0.8%, the elderly outnumber the young for the first time. Implications on AVS, LPP and welfare.

## In a nutshell - Population 9,127 million at 31/12/2025: growth +0.8% (slowdown vs 1.0% 2024) - Elderly (65+) outnumber young people (<20) for the first time: 1,810,600 vs 1,804,500 - Migration balance falls by 14.9%; internal mobility falls (56 vs 61 displacements per 1,000 inhabitants) - Migration down 3.9%, emigration up 3.1% compared to 2024
## Key facts - **What**: Definitive demographic data 2025 from the Federal Statistical Office - When: 31 December 2025 (press release 20 August 2026) - Where: Switzerland, all 26 cantons - Who: UST (Federal Statistical Office) - Inhabitants: 9,127,100 (+0.8% per year) - Elderly (65+): 1,810,600 (outnumber young people <20 for the first time) - Migration balance: 70,400 (-14.9% compared to 2024)
Switzerland closes 2025 with 9,127,100 permanent residents. According to the final data of the Federal Statistical Office (FSO), population growth continues but at a significantly slower pace: +0.8% compared to 2024 (+1.0%) and 2023 (+1.7%). This slowdown reflects a year characterized by less immigration and more emigration, confirming the trends observed in the provisional data released in April 2026.
The profile of the population is transformed. Among the 9,127 million inhabitants, 6,599,000 have Swiss nationality (72%), while 2,528,100 are foreigners (28%). In 2025, the Swiss population grew by 27,900 people (+0.4%), while the foreign population increased by 48,200 people (+1.9%). ### Internal mobility on the decline Alongside comprehensive demographic data, the UST has provided information on population mobility within the Swiss territory. In 2025, 511,200 internal migrations were recorded: 358,000 intracantonal (within the same canton) and 153,200 intercantonal (between different cantons). When related to the number of inhabitants, these numbers highlight a trend of slowdown: only 56 movements per 1,000 inhabitants in 2025, compared to 61 per 1,000 inhabitants ten years earlier. This decline in internal mobility affects both nationality groups, albeit in different ways. In 2025, foreign people maintain a higher mobility compared to Swiss citizens (80 movements per 1,000 foreigners, against 47 per 1,000 Swiss citizens). However, it is precisely among Swiss citizens that the decline in mobility is more marked from 2021 onwards, suggesting growing residential stability or possible economic constraints related to housing costs. ### Pension system under pressure The UST's demographic data has direct repercussions on the sustainability of the Swiss pension system. When the elderly surpass the young, the ratio between active contributors and pensioners narrows, exerting financial pressure on AVS (Old Age Insurance) and LPP (Professional Pension). The natural population growth (only 8% of total growth in 2025) suggests that Switzerland will still rely on migratory balance for many years to maintain an adequate number of active workers. However, the decline in migratory balance in 2025 (-14.9%) indicates that this source of supply is weakening. At the territorial level, the 17 cantons with an older population will face more consistent welfare, health, and long-term care needs, while the nine cantons with younger demographic profiles can count on a broader contributory base. Consult our tools to verify your pension position. The variability between cantons suggests that demographic pressures are not uniform: Vaud, Geneva, Fribourg, and Zurich still maintain younger profiles, while other regions will face more acute sustainability challenges. ### Nationality and labor market dynamics The decline in immigration (-3.9% compared to 2024) and the increase in emigration (+3.1%) indicate changes in the attractive forces of the Swiss labor market. Among new immigrants, Germans remain the largest group (12.9% of flows), followed by Swiss returnees (11.3%), French (10.1%), and Italians (9.1%). On the other hand, Swiss emigration (22% of those leaving the country) suggests a search for opportunities abroad, while that of Portuguese, Italians, and French may reflect economic changes in their countries of origin. These migratory flows have direct effects on the Swiss labor market: fewer immigrants mean less labor supply for certain sectors (construction, hospitality, healthcare), but also less pressure on Swiss citizens' salaries, at least in the short term. With a growing life expectancy and an increasingly unfavorable ratio between active and pensioners, it is essential not to rely solely on the AVS guarantee. The contribution rates for the second pillar (LPP) vary by age group: from 7% between 25 and 34 years, to 10% between 35 and 44 years, to 15% between 45 and 54 years, up to 18% after 55 years up to the reference age. These tools allow for federal and cantonal tax deductions, reducing the tax burden while accumulating additional capital for retirement.
### Cost of living and housing dynamics The slowdown in demographic growth does not necessarily mean a decline in the cost of living in Switzerland. Rather, aging of the population implies a reconfiguration of housing demand: fewer expanding family units, more pensioners seeking housing solutions tailored to their needs. This phenomenon is reflected in property prices and rents at the local level, with marked variations between cantons. The cantons with the youngest population (Vaud, Geneva, Fribourg, Zurich) are likely to continue exerting pressure on prices, while those with more elderly populations may see emerging housing opportunities at a lower price.

This trend may reflect a greater difficulty in finding accessible housing in other regions, or a greater preference for telework and flexibility. For employers, it means that the local pool of competitive talent is reduced, prompting them to invest more in internal training and job attractiveness.
Those looking for work in Switzerland should take advantage of this trend: the relative scarcity of mobile candidates amplifies personal bargaining power. It is advisable to negotiate flexibility in working hours, telework, performance bonuses, and salary supplements. ## Key facts - **What**: Marked recovery of Swiss foreign trade after months of stagnation - When: July 2026 (official statement of August 20, 2026) - Where: Switzerland, national level - Who: Swiss Federal Administration - Exports: +13.8% in monthly variation (seasonally adjusted) - Imports: -4.5% in monthly variation (seasonally adjusted) - Trade balance surplus: +8.1 billion CHF (new monthly record) - Driving sector: Chemical-pharmaceutical
### Net rebound after the stagnation period
In July 2026, Swiss foreign trade experienced a very mixed development, but decidedly favourable overall. In seasonally adjusted terms, exports reached a net increase of 13.8 percent compared to the previous month, while at the same time imports suffered a decrease of 4.5 percent. This divergent dynamic between outbound and inbound trade flows produced a direct and positive effect on the trade balance, which reached a new monthly record of 8.1 billion Swiss francs.
The relevant aspect is that the official source explicitly reports a "recovery in exports after months of stagnation". This means that the period ### What does the recovery mean for the Swiss economy
The recovery of exports after months of stagnation represents a significant change in trend for the Swiss economy as a whole. A 13.8 percent increase in monthly variation, even after seasonal adjustment, indicates a more vibrant international demand for Swiss products. At the same time, the 4.5 percent contraction in imports signals an asymmetric evolution: foreign markets are pulling more strongly towards Swiss goods, while domestic demand for imported goods is decreasing. This favorable imbalance directly generates a record trade surplus, which represents a valuable source of currency for the Swiss economic system and has a positive impact on foreign accounts.
### Implications for the Swiss franc exchange rate
A consistent trade surplus traditionally exercises upward pressure on the national currency. In the Swiss case, the July surplus of 8.1 billion francs may contribute to a progressive strengthening of the CHF against major currencies, including the EUR. For border residents who earn in euros and spend in Swiss francs, a stronger franc means a reduction in purchasing power in daily purchases, rents, healthcare expenses, and Swiss services in the medium to long term. Those who maintain euro savings suffer similarly from a relative loss of value in the exchange rate.
To monitor these effects, it is useful to regularly consult the data on the CHF/EUR exchange rate and official economic indicators published by UST/BFS.
### The pharmaceutical-chemical sector as the driving force of the recovery
The fact that the pharmaceutical-chemical sector is the main driver of both exports and imports in July 2026 highlights the central role that this sector plays in the Swiss economy. It is one of the pillars of the Swiss industrial system, characterized by massive investments in research and development, the production of high-tech pharmaceuticals with a very high technological content, and a sophisticated global network of suppliers and customers. The recovery in this sector is indicative of a renewed dynamics in international trade of high-tech and high-value-added products.
For those working in Switzerland, especially in the industrial and pharmaceutical-chemical sectors, the July commercial recovery represents a positive signal of occupational stability and potential growth in the following quarters. However, a single monthly data point does not allow us to affirm that the trend is definitively reversed: it will be necessary to monitor the subsequent data (August, September, October) to assess the sustainability of the recovery and to understand if it will extend to other sectors beyond the pharmaceutical-chemical sector.

For those who want to stay up-to-date on the evolution of the Swiss economy and foreign trade dynamics, it's useful to know where to access official data. The Swiss Federal Administration (admin.ch) publishes detailed press releases on a monthly basis with export and import data, divided by economic sector, partner country, and Swiss region of origin. The Federal Statistical Office (UST/BFS) also makes available complete datasets and interactive visualization platforms, allowing users to download raw data, compare periods, and analyze specific trends by sector.
Data is published with a delay of approximately 20 days from the end of the reference month. In the case of July 2026, the press release was published on August 20. This regular and predictable schedule allows workers, entrepreneurs, investors, economists, and policymakers to monitor the national foreign trade situation and make informed assessments.
### What to Watch Out for in the Coming Months
In the following articles and economic analyses, it's worth paying attention to three key elements:
- **Sustainability of the Recovery**: Data from August and September 2026 will confirm the recovery, or was it a temporary and isolated rebound? - Expansion of the Momentum: Will the recovery extend beyond the pharmaceutical-chemical sector to other Swiss economic sectors (precision mechanics, watchmaking, textiles, food, etc.)? - Indirect Effects on Employment: How will the labor market, unemployment rate, and wage negotiation possibilities respond in the short and medium term?
### Practical Tools for Border Workers and Swiss Workers
For border workers and those working in Switzerland, a sustained economic recovery means stability of income, reduced risk of unemployment, and potential improvement of contract and salary conditions. It's useful to regularly consult the official SECO data on employment and the labor market for an integrated view, as foreign trade and employment are closely linked: when exports grow, companies hire.
Additionally, those managing savings or pension plans (AVS/AHV, LPP/BVG, third pillar 3a) may find it useful to monitor the Swiss franc's performance: a stronger CHF directly affects the valuation of portfolios with foreign currency positions and diversification strategies.

item.title: Residence permit B Schaffhausen: requirements and renewal
item.description: Permit B is a renewable permit to reside and work in Switzerland, managed by SEM. Find out how to get it and renew it in the canton of Schaffhausen.

## In a nutshell - Renewable residence permit to reside and work in Switzerland - Managed by SEM (State Secretariat for Migration) - Valid for workers and dependent family members - Renewable at the end of validity
## Key facts - **What**: Residence permit category B - Type: Renewable (non-permanent) - Who manages: SEM (State Secretariat for Migration) - Where: Canton Schaffhausen - Validity: Determined on a case-by-case basis by the cantonal authorities
The category B residence permit is one of the four main residence permits in Switzerland and is intended for those who intend to reside and work in the country for a medium-long period. Unlike the [L short-term permit](/nav:health), which is limited to one year, the B permit offers greater stability. At the same time, it differs from the residence permit C, reserved for those who achieve specific integration and permanence requirements.
The canton of Schaffhausen, like all Swiss cantons, administers the practices related to residence permits according to the federal regulations established by the SEM. This means that procedures, required documents and deadlines follow a national framework, although the cantonal migration office remains the direct point of contact for residents and applicants.
### Nature and characteristics of permit B
Permit B is defined as a «renewable residence», which implies that it is not a definitive permit but an authorization that expires ## Access requirements and policies
The requirements for obtaining and maintaining a B permit in Switzerland follow federally established criteria. Although the SEM defines the general framework, the cantonal migration office of Schaffhausen assesses each application considering the individual situation of the applicant.
A central element for obtaining the B permit is the availability of a verified job offer. This means that you generally need to have an employment contract or a promise of employment from an employer located in the canton (or Switzerland in general). The migration office will verify that the employment relationship is legitimate and that the salary complies with Swiss market standards. This check is part of the so-called labour market review, aimed at ensuring that the permit does not replace jobs for Swiss residents.
Another relevant aspect concerns the financial and social situation. Applicants must demonstrate that they can support themselves through their earned income. In addition, Switzerland requires that those staying in the country have [health insurance coverage (LAMal)](/nav:health), which is mandatory for all residents within three months of arrival. The lack of such insurance may result in complications in the granting or renewal of the permit.

The renewal of permit B must be started before the expiration of the current validity. There is no fixed date at national level; the time of renewal depends on the expiry date indicated on the permit itself. As a rule, it is advisable to contact the cantonal migration office at least two or three months before the deadline, so that you have enough time to collect the documentation and complete the procedure.
The documentation required for renewal is similar to that submitted for the initial application:
- Renewal request form (available at the cantonal office or on the official site of the canton Schaffhausen) - Updated employment contract or letter from the employer attesting to the continuity of employment - Certificate of payment of social contributions (AVS/AHV) and health insurance coverage (LAMal) - Valid ID or passport - Certificate of absence of criminal convictions (sometimes required, depending on the circumstances) - Certification of a permanent residence (lease or certificate of ownership)
With regard to social contributions, each employee in Switzerland pays 5.3% of AVS/AI/IPG contributions and an amount for unemployment insurance. The continuity of these payments is an element that the migration office checks to ascertain the stability of the situation.
